1

  • N: [ā]nu | pâša | īpušam-[ma]
  • T: Anu [made ready] to speak,
  • L: [ā]nu ← Anu I “An(um) (the god of heaven) OAkk, Bab.”; pâša ← pû I “(also OB)”; īpušam-[ma] ← epēšu II “to do”

2

  • T: And said to [his brother, Enlil],

SipNB1 o 2. [iz-za]-ak-kar₃ a-na a-hi-šu {d}+en-[lil₂]

3

  • N: [siq]ra | ša igīgī || iphurūni | ab-bābišk[a]
  • T: “The reason why the Igigi-gods gathered at your gate,
  • L: [siq]ra ← zikru I “jB st. constr. siqar utterance”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; igīgī ← Igigû I “the (ten) great gods O/jB”; iphurūni ← pahāru II “to gather”; ab-bābišk[a] ← ana I, bābu I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”
  • Note: See [RN118: 185]: “The mundane iphurūnim replaces the more vivid ilmû (OB I 114). In translating siqra we follow Lambert (also Bottéro, Foster); another such use of the word may be in OB Gilgameš II (P) 141–2: a-na mi-nim il-li#-kam si₂-qi-ir-šu lu-uš#-me!(šu), ‘why he came here, I would hear his reason’.”
  • Note: The sign is a clear UN (not a compressed -nim a- as copied by Al-Rawi), perhaps an apocopated form of the ventive.

7

  • T: “Nusku, open [your] gate,
  • L: [nusku] ← Nusku I; pite ← petû II “to open”; bābka ← bābu I “pl. m. & f. gate, door”

8

  • N: k[ak]kīka | liqe || ṣi | ap-puhri
  • T: “Take your weapons and go out to the group,
  • L: k[ak]kīka ← kakku I “stick”; liqe ← leqû II “to take, take over”; ṣi ← aṣû I “to go out, + vent. come out (from = ina, ištu, acc.)”; ap-puhri ← ana I, puhru I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”
  • Note: See [RN118: 185]: “The plene writing of the first vowel in li-i-qe₂ (II 8) is unwanted, but reveals that for one LB scribe, at least, the I/1 imperative of leqû followed the pattern of limad and rikab (also pišah, tikal, tišab, etc.) rather than mahaṣ. Among verbs III-weak (e), of course, the pattern followed by the imperative in Babylonian is usually uncertain because of the ambiguities of script: e.g. pete or pite, šeme or šime, ṭehe or ṭihe? (cf. [RN27201: §105 f]). Verbs III-weak (a) with attested I/1 imperatives are rare, but kila is standard and tima (Bab.) is found alongside tama (Ass.); note also OA kita < katā'um. On this evidence, slim though it is, the pattern limad appears to be typical of such verbs, and presumably ought to be of verbs III-weak (e) also. Accordingly the spelling li-i-qe₂ might be taken as orthographic evidence for an imperative liqe in preference to leqe, though obviously it would be foolish to insist that a variant leqe never occurred.”
SipNB1 o 8. k[a-ak]-ki#-ka li-i-qe₂ ṣi-i ap-pu-uh₂#-ri#

32

  • N: ibbalkitū | hupšu | issi
  • T: They were defiant, the labor gang cried out,
  • L: ibbalkitū ← nabalkutu II “to cross over”; hupšu ← hupšu I “(member of) lower class esp. MA, Alal. (Hurr. pl. hupšena), Am.,…”; issi ← šasû I “to shout, call (out)”
  • Note: See [RN118: 185]: “In the synonym list Explicit Malku II [N.B. now edited by [RN500: 290–291]] the word hupšu is equated with nišu ([temp_id_2401129561684543 442: j]), and in a commentary on Šumma ālu, with ṣābū(ERIN₂-MEŠ) [x] ([UBHD-LS: 140] @url{/fragmentarium/K.4229}{K.4229}, 12). These equivalences indicate only that hupšu refers to a group of people. In the army the hupšu is indeed the mass of common soldiers, but more relevant to our passage is its use to denote a labour gang engaged in public works, as in the omen apodosis tīb hup₂-ši mar-ri u tup-ši-[ik-ki], “mutiny of spade-gang and basket-gang” ([RN2605: 442, rev. 2]), and in an inscription of Sargon II: [...] eṭlūti(GURUŠ)-MEŠ-šu₂ il-ku tup-šik-ku mar-ṣi-iš u₂# im-ta-ni ṣāb(ERIN₂)-MEŠ hup-šiš, “[he imposed on] his male population the grievous burden of corvée-work and basket-carrying, [and] counted them among the labour gang” ([UBHD-1553949: 1, 33]). The curious plene writing of the first syllable is also found in the line of Explicit Malku cited above: [hu]-u₂-up-šu.”

  • L: ila ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; ištēn ← ištēn I “f. išteat, ištiat, iš/ltē/īt(um), iš/ltât, NA issēt”; šisī-ma ← šasû I “to shout, call (out)”; [lū ← lū I “let it be”; ut]eddušū? ← edēšu I “to be(come) new”; parṣū ← parṣu I “office”
  • Note: In the old excavation photo of SipNB1 the sign before šu₂ has two clear Winkelhaken before the vertical, which render it incompatible with a reading DI (cf. [RN118: 186]), but also with the DU of MS NinNA1. Cf. [RN118: 186]: “In I. 60 the new tablet and collation of MS M reveals that the final word is parṣi. The line no longer appears explicitly to recommend the death of the strikers’ leader, as previously understood. The slaughter of a god is thus first mentioned specifically in SB II 91, where it is the suggestion of Ea. Here, Enlil’s proposal is less easy to determine, since we are handicapped by the manuscripts' disagreement over the verb. MS M has [l]iddûšu (pl., nadû), with the Anunnaki as a plausible subject, but the new tablet appears to have liddīšu (sing., nadû), which does not yield good sense, or liddišū, “let them renew” (pl., edēšu), which does. Not enough of MS L survives to know how the verb stood in that source. The Assyrian recension possibly has the imperative of nadû (MS S ii 7: i-d[i-šu?]). In the reading offered by the Sippar tablet, we assume that Enlil’s wish is for the Anunnaki, here the great decision-making gods, to set about establishing a new order in the universe (parṣī uddušu). This is necessary because he himself has abdicated in favour of Anu. However, the search for the instigator of the conflict that began with Nuska’s mission is not to be given up. But there is a difficulty: because the mutinous gods have unanimously accepted joint responsibility for their strike, no one individual can be identified as prime mover. Accordingly, Enlil proposes that Anu summon “a certain god” (ilam ištēn), that is, any one of his choosing from among the rebels, into the presence of the divine council, which will, implicitly, decide his fate and in doing so establish a new order. The reading preserved on the Kuyunjik manuscript, liddûšu, is open to a similar interpretation. The meaning of parṣi nadû is clear from the myth of Anzû, where the phrase describes the overturning of the natural order that follows Enlil’s involuntary loss of his powers (@url{corpus/L/1/10/OB/II#1}{OB Anzû II 1}: {den-lil₂-lu-tam i-te-ki-im na-du-u₂ pa-ar-ṣu₂}, “he snatched the Enlilship, the divine regulations were cast down”; cf. @url{corpus/L/1/10/SB/I#b%2B78}{SB Anzû I 81}: {den-lil₂-u₂-ta il-te-qe₂ na-du-u₂ [par-ṣu]}). In the present context this is perhaps a possible idiom, literally “let them cast down the divine regulations for him.” The natural order of things will be set aside to allow the punishing of one of the rebels, and thereafter re-established.” See also: [RN630: 56]: “Die Lesung [RN435: 52, 151]: ... l[i-id-du-šu₂ tam-ta ist obsolet, s.a. [pettinato1970review: 78–79], [moran1970creation: 52 Anm. 13]. Der Ausdruck parṣī nadû in [173] M könnte nach [RN118: 186] dieselbe Bedeutung von parṣī uddušu in Si haben: das Niederlegen einer bestehenden göttlichen Ordnung, die nach der Bestrafung eines Gottes wieder hergestellt wird.” Wilcke ([RN1196: 77 with fn. 25]) understands the line (reading nadû) as “Ruf (den) einen Gott! Sie sollen ihm mein Amt auferlegen!”

104

  • N: a[lla] | ellil || iṭbuhūšu | mahrīti
  • T: Alla, an Enlil of former time (?).
  • L: a[lla] ← Alla I; ellil ← Ellil I “”; iṭbuhūšu ← ṭabāhu I “to slaughter”; mahrīti ← mahrû I “f. mahrītu(m)”
  • Note: See [RN118: 187]: “This line replaces older ina puhrīšunu iṭṭabḫū (OB I 224 [= 220]). The syntax is again in disarray, with the verb iṭbuḫūšu intruding into the unity of the possessive construction, Ellil maḫrītim (if maḫrītim seems unconvincing one may read iṭbuhūšūma aḫrīti, but since the plural mahrâtu can mean “former times” there seems to us no reason why the singular should not also carry this meaning; cf. the attested analogous pairs aḫrītu : aḫrâtu, arkītu : arkâtu, pānītu : pānâtu). The phrase “an Enlil of old”, meaning a god who was once a senior figure but who later lost his position, is comparable with “the Enlils who rebelled” ({den.lil₂.la₂{meš}} ša₂ ik-kir-[u₂]) and “the seven conquered Enlils” (7 {den.lil₂{meš}} ki-šit-ti || 7 dingir.dingir dingir{meš} (= {dil₃-il₃-MEŠ?}) ki-šit-tu₄) of mythology, and among these, equated with Anšar, Alla was indeed numbered: see [lambert1980theology: 65] (the passages there cited have been recently edited by [RN383: 155, 17; 194; 198, rev. 8]). If the syntactical disorder of this line is not simply corrupt, we can only suggest that it is intended to highlight the shocking deed retailed. To our knowledge the most obvious parallel is in Enūma eliš I 81–2, where the great significance of the event described the birth of Marduk induces the poet to repeat the crucial line with an added adjective violating the unity of the possessive construction: ina qe₂-reb apsî(abzu) ib-ba-ni [{dmar]duk} / ina qe₂-reb elli(ku₃) apsî(abzu) ib-ba-ni [{dmarduk}].”
  • Note: The name of Enlil is preserved in the fragment copied in [RN118: 169].
